title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E740 looks for space curves, given by two projections y = y(x) and z = z(x), that extremize ∫V dx. Here V = V(x, y, z, p, p', q, q', r, r', ...), with p = y', q = y'', r = y''' and p' = z', q' = z'', r' = z'''. The previous page wrote the differential as dV = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + N' dz + P' dp' + Q' dq' + R' dr' + ... and recalled Euler's earlier single-function result (Methodus inveniendi, 1744): N - dP/dx + d²Q/dx² - d³R/dx³ + ... = 0.

§7 (this page): Euler treats the projection z(x) as already known, i.e. fixed. Then z, p', q', r' are known functions of x, and all terms N'dz + P'dp' + Q'dq' + R'dr' can be absorbed into the M dx term. Since M never enters the final equation, the ordinary one-function method gives the equation for y: N - dP/dx + d²Q/dx² - d³R/dx³ = 0.

§8: Symmetrically, Euler fixes y(x). The terms N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr go into M dx, which gives N' - dP'/dx + d²Q'/dx² - d³R'/dx³ = 0.

§9: When neither projection is known, both equations I and II must hold together. In modern terms this is the Euler–Lagrange system for a functional of two dependent variables with higher-order derivatives. The argument is sound: any extremal must be extremal under variations of each component separately, which gives necessary conditions. The page does not address sufficiency or boundary conditions.

The next page goes on to the first-order case, N dx = dP and N' dx = dP'. It then derives the first integral d(V - pP - p'P') = M dx, a Beltrami/Hamiltonian-type identity.
errors: Printed misprint, end of §7: the last term is printed as ∂³R/∂x² and should be ∂³R/∂x³.
Printed misprint, §8: the equation is printed with unprimed Q and R (∂∂Q/∂x², ∂³R/∂x³) and should read Q', R'. It is correct in §9 II.
Minor gap: the 'fix one function, vary the other' argument yields necessary conditions only. Boundary/endpoint conditions and sufficiency are not discussed. This is standard for the period.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equations for a functional of several dependent functions, here the two projections of a space curve, derived by freezing one function and applying the single-function rule to the other.
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange system for vector-valued unknowns (with higher derivatives, Euler–Poisson equations)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744 for one function; spatial cases partly treated there); Lagrange (1760s, δ-method, several functions)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65, 1744) for the one-function formula; the extension to several functions is standard after Lagrange. E740 itself is posthumous (1813, Mémoires St Petersburg).

ideas.what: Absorbing all terms involving the 'known' function into the M dx term, noting M does not enter the final equation.
ideas.modern_name: Treating explicit x-dependence as irrelevant to the Euler–Lagrange operator

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine, correct derivation of the Euler–Lagrange system for two unknown functions, which was well known by 1813 through Lagrange. The only peculiarities are two printing misprints.
transcription_corrections: §7 final equation: the image indeed shows ∂³R/∂x² (a printed misprint), so the transcription is faithful to the print.
Line 7 of the page: the image reads 'M∂x' / 'Mdx' inconsistently ('in membro Mdx'). The transcription matches.
§8 equation: the image shows unprimed Q and R in the last two terms, matching the transcription (a printed misprint).
